nameStory: The Ubiquitous Peaclam gets its name from its tiny size - these freshwater clams are about as small as a pea! The word 'ubiquitous' means found everywhere, though ironically this little clam is quite uncommon in our New England waters despite its grand name.
description: The Ubiquitous Peaclam is a tiny freshwater bivalve mollusk that most people overlook completely. These miniature clams have two hinged shells that can snap shut, just like their larger ocean cousins, but they're small enough to sit comfortably on your fingernail. They're among the smallest clams in North America, rarely growing larger than a small pea. Despite being called 'ubiquitous,' they're actually quite rare finds in New England's freshwater habitats.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small - typically pea-sized or smaller, easily fitting on your fingernail with room to spare

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Nearly round with two matching halves that hinge together, feeling smooth and hard like a tiny ceramic bead

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Usually pale yellowish-brown to grayish-white, sometimes with a subtle pearlescent sheen when wet

idTips.label: Habitat Location
idTips.description: Found buried in soft mud or sand at the bottom of ponds, slow streams, or lake edges

idTips.label: Shell Texture
idTips.description: Smooth, glossy surface that feels slippery when wet and makes a tiny 'click' sound when tapped gently

habitat: Look for Ubiquitous Peaclams in the muddy or sandy bottoms of quiet freshwater areas like ponds, slow-moving streams, and shallow lake margins. They prefer soft sediments where they can burrow and filter-feed on microscopic particles in the water. In New England, they're most likely found in lowland waters with gentle currents and plenty of organic matter in the substrate.

seasonality.spring: Active and feeding as waters warm, though you'll need to sift through bottom sediments carefully to spot their tiny shells.
seasonality.summer: Most active period for feeding and reproduction, but still requires patient searching through pond and stream bottom materials.
seasonality.fall: Beginning to slow down but still present, often easier to find as water levels drop and concentrate them in smaller areas.
seasonality.winter: Dormant in bottom sediments under ice, virtually impossible to locate without disturbing their muddy refuges.

funFact: These tiny clams are actually living water purifiers - a single peaclam can filter several gallons of water per day through its miniature body, cleaning microscopic algae and bacteria from the water as it feeds!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with small snail shells or even seeds and pebbles due to their tiny size. Unlike snails, peaclams have two symmetrical shell halves that open and close, while snail shells are spiral-shaped. Remember: if it has a hinge, it's a clam!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'ubiquitous' (meaning everywhere), this species is actually quite uncommon in New England, making any discovery special. The scientific name 'casertana' refers to the Italian region where it was first scientifically described, showing how these tiny travelers have spread across continents.
compareHints: Since this is the only Euglesa species recorded in our dataset for New England, compare it with other small freshwater clams in the pea clam family. Other peaclams might be slightly different in shape or color, but all share that characteristic tiny size and bivalve shell structure. The Ubiquitous Peaclam tends to be more perfectly round than its relatives, which may be more oval or elongated.
